title: The Unanimous Vote
subtitle: Love & Duty · Chapter 41 of 50
content:
The day the Lanternweald asked us for help, Toph broke a different chair.

This one belonged to the community hall.

“It had it coming,” she said.

Katara looked at the splintered backrest, then at Toph, then at me.

“I don't suppose this is a structural assessment?”

“It is now.”

Aang had brought us across the Riverstone Door after receiving Neri's message about cargo arriving in the wrong places. He'd arrived expecting to help move parcels and discovered that somebody had called an emergency meeting. The meeting included seven people, four clipboards, two incomplete inventories, and a tray of buns Greg had brought because nobody should have to argue on an empty stomach.

I was impressed by how quickly this little corner of the universe had learned bureaucracy.

Aang unfolded the map in the center of the table. “If the doors are carrying people safely, that's important. But supplies going astray could still hurt someone.”

“Already almost did,” Katara said. She was sorting the records for a jar of medicine that had taken an accidental detour through Jasmine Steps. The jar was sealed, intact, and now exactly where it belonged. That didn't erase the hour she'd spent waiting for it.

Toph dragged a finger along the diagram of the bell's rings.

“Somebody bent this.”

“Maybe the mechanism wore out,” Aang said.

“Metal doesn't wear into measurement marks.”

He blinked. “Right.”

She grinned. “It's okay, Twinkle Toes. We all have limitations.”

He smiled back, but I could see he was watching the door. There were people in Cranefish Town who needed him, and he hated being away when somebody might require a decision.

I touched his sleeve.

“Don't solve the entire vale before lunch.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“You were making the face.”

“What face?”

“The face where the Avatar is about to volunteer everyone for something.”

Toph laughed. Katara did not, which meant she agreed with me even more.

Neri told us about the seventh brass ring, a part of the mechanism that moved only when the other six fell out of alignment. It did not grant wishes or summon people. It kept track of unresolved transfers, although nobody had maintained the ledger rigorously since the old keepers died.

Aang wanted to help the well recover by opening every door and asking travelers to bring the lost things home.

Katara shook her head before he finished. “That's more movement through an already strained system.”

“Then we close them?”

“Also no. The clinic needs the Moonroot supplies.”

Toph knocked her knuckles against the table. “Ask the people who use the doors what they can spare. Stop guessing.”

“I thought we were asking,” Aang said.

“We're three minutes into a meeting you didn't know existed,” I said. “We can improve.”

He looked genuinely wounded.

That made me love him a little more.

The four of us stepped outside while Neri copied the inventory. Riverstone Terrace smelled of hot stone, cut wood, and the stew someone was making for the repair crews. Aang sat on the low wall. Katara stood beside him, arms folded. Toph leaned against me with the kind of casual confidence she refused to acknowledge as affection.

I looked at all three.

“We know how to do this part,” I said. “Not perfectly. But we've had practice.”

“Household agreements,” Katara said.

“Separate money,” Toph added.

“Shared expenses,” Aang said. “And no volunteering somebody else's labor.”

He gave me a rueful look.

“Especially that last one,” I agreed.

The first thing we did was stop calling the problem the Lanternwell's failure. It was a shared obligation with actual names attached. Somebody had written a new set of destination labels. Somebody had changed the order of the supplies. Somebody would need help making things right.

The second thing we did was refuse to put Jasper, Aang, Katara, and Toph into one category marked ‘four votes.’

“I want four,” I told Neri when we returned.

She hesitated. “Four what?”

“Four people. Four opinions. It doesn't matter that we share a house.”

Toph lifted her chin. “And I reserve the right to call the other three idiots.”

“Accepted,” Katara said.

Aang considered. “Can I reserve that right?”

“No,” said Toph.

The meeting became useful after that.

Katara described what the clinic required and what could wait. Toph offered to inspect the rings but refused to promise a permanent repair before seeing the damage. Aang agreed to work on a safe way of separating the water channel from the wheels. I volunteered to build a written distribution plan that would not require anyone to memorize which world somebody's herbs came from.

Greg had a question.

“What if a person doesn't want their name on a list?”

A fair point. I set down my pencil.

“Then they can designate somebody they trust to account for the parcel. Nobody has to explain where they came from or who they love just to borrow a hammer.”

I meant it practically. I also meant it more deeply than I had expected.

Katara met my gaze across the table. She knew that look. So did Toph.

Aang nodded slowly. “A record of responsibilities, not identities.”

“Exactly.”

The last motion concerned the labels. Neri proposed that each district approve a single contact before deliveries crossed a Threadway. It sounded tidy. It also sounded like the first page of a rulebook that could make ordinary people ask permission to help one another.

“We need a way for someone to send an emergency,” Katara said.

“And a way to refuse one,” I added.

“Both,” Aang agreed.

Toph leaned forward. “And somebody who's allowed to tell the person running the system that the system's stupid.”

“Certainly,” Neri said, dry as dust. “I shall put your name in the margin.”

“You'll need a whole page.”

We voted. Not unanimously.

The proposal needed revision.

That was its first honest success.

By late afternoon, the broken chair was repaired. Toph had restored the join with the same care she gave a complicated piece of metal. She rubbed her palms together as though it had not mattered.

Katara went to find the person who'd missed a meal. Aang helped string a temporary line to catch crates that slid out of place. Toph stayed beside me at the table, listening to the scratch of my pen.

“You know the scary thing?” she asked.

“That you're about to make a speech?”

“That you're good at this.”

“Rude.”

She nudged my boot with hers. “Don't let them turn you into another committee.”

“I'll try.”

The others came back smelling of bread, river water, and the kind of day's work that has no ending bell. Aang pressed a kiss to my hair. Katara kissed my cheek. Toph made a disapproving noise until I caught her hand under the table.

We stayed to eat.

Later, as we walked toward the Riverstone Door, Aang showed me a copy of the amended motion.

At the bottom was a note in an unfamiliar hand:

THE KEEPERS ALREADY HAD A BETTER SYSTEM. YOU BROKE IT BY ASKING TOO MANY PEOPLE.

I read it twice.

Toph took the page and ran her fingers across the pressed writing.

“Whoever wrote this,” she said, “really hates being told no.”

Katara folded the note.

“Then they'll have to learn.”

Aang looked back at the Lanternwell. He didn't offer to solve it alone.

He asked what we should do tomorrow.
